findings.where: Ranking method section, the four body paragraphs under its single h2 (payment, the pull toward the area average, which reviews count, review count and sorting). Worst at phone width, where they run about one and a half screens.
findings.fault: Four separate answers sit under one heading as unbroken body text. Nothing in the type marks where one topic ends and the next begins: no subheads and no bold lead-ins. The long paragraphs, of seven and eight lines on desktop and more on a phone, read as one grey block.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker who doubts a ranking site reads this page on a phone to answer one question, such as 'can a hostel pay to rank higher?' or 'why does this place with 3 reviews score so well?'. They have to read the whole block to find the paragraph that answers it, and many will give up before they do. That defeats a page whose job is to make the ranking easy to check and trust.

findings.where: Intro, the paragraph between the lede and the numbered list ('Scores weight toward recent stays...')
findings.fault: The intro steps down from the large lede to body size halfway through. Set in body size, the summary sentence reads as the first paragraph of the body rather than part of the intro. The three-item list after it then looks like it belongs to the body too, not like the page's summary.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who skims the top of the page for the short version cannot see where the summary ends and the detail begins. They may read the whole intro as body text and miss the three-line answer it gives.

findings.where: Scoring method, the decay list (100%, 50%, 25%), and the intro list of three principles
findings.fault: Both lists use numerals. In the decay list, the numbers 1, 2 and 3 sit beside 100%, 50% and 25%, so two sets of figures compete. The only figures on the page sit at the ends of sentences, set the same as the words around them. In the intro list, the numbers suggest a sequence or ranking among three principles that have no order.
findings.who_objects: A visitor scanning for 'how much does an old review count?' meets the list numbers before the percentages. The figures the section exists to give do not stand out from the sentences around them.
